model_answers.transcript:
I will talk about one day last year when we wanted to go to the beach. It was in the summer, and I planned it with my two cousins.

So the plan was, we go to the coast for the whole day. My aunt has a car and she said she can drive us there. We packed everything the night before, the food and the towels and all of this. We are very excited because we don't go there so much.

But then in the morning there is a big storm. I wake up and the rain is very heavy, and my aunt looked at her phone and she said the road to the coast is closed. So we cannot go. I felt very disappointing at that moment, and my cousins also.

So we stayed in the house. We cooked together and we played cards, and actually it was very nice. We talked a lot, more than normally. So in the end it was good, maybe better than the beach. model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a day last August, when the four of us were supposed to drive down to the coast and never got there.

The plan had been in the diary for weeks. My aunt was going to drive, and my two cousins and I had spent the previous evening loading the car — food, towels, the lot — so that we could leave at seven and get a full day out of it. We hardly ever manage to go anywhere together, so it had built up into a bit of an occasion.

What actually happened was that a storm came in overnight. I woke up at about six to rain hammering on the window, and by the time I got downstairs my aunt had already checked and the coast road was shut. There wasn't much to discuss, really. Nobody was going to drive two hours through that on the off chance it reopened.

As for how it turned out — better than the trip would have been, if I'm honest. We ended up in my aunt's kitchen for the whole day, cooking far more food than four people needed, and we got through about six games of cards. My cousins and I talked more in that one afternoon than we had in a year, and that wouldn't have happened on a crowded beach. If the weather had held, we'd have spent half the day in traffic and come home sunburnt and quiet.

Looking back, the weather did us a favour. The trip was only ever the excuse to be in the same room.

model_answers.transcript:
This is about a day last August that was meant to be spent at the coast and wasn't.

We'd had it planned for the best part of a month — my aunt driving, my two cousins and me, an early start so we'd get the whole day out of it. The car was loaded the night before, which tells you how seriously we were taking it. We're scattered all over the country now, so a day at the sea had quietly turned into something rather more than a day at the sea.

Then a storm blew in overnight. I was woken at six by rain coming down like gravel on the glass, and by the time I'd got downstairs my aunt had checked and the road was shut. Nobody argued about it. There's no sense in driving two hours into weather like that on the strength of a maybe.

What we did instead was very little, and that was rather the point. We stayed in the kitchen, cooked enough for twice our number, and played cards until it got dark. Had we made it to the coast, we'd have spent half of it queuing and the other half hunting for somewhere to park.

The odd thing is that I can't remember a single beach day from that whole decade, and I can remember that kitchen exactly. I've come round to the view that a plan is often just a pretext for getting everybody in the same room, and that the weather occasionally does you the favour of removing the pretext.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my boots. They are walking boots, brown colour, and they are made from leather. I bought them maybe nine years ago because I was going to do a long walk in the mountains.

I have them since that time and I use them very much, not only for the mountains but also in winter for normal days. They are very good boots. After some years the bottom part, the sole, it was broken. There was a hole and my foot is wet every time I go outside.

So I take them to a small shop near the station. The man there said he can fix it. He put a new sole and it took one week. It cost me forty pounds. And after that I did the same thing again two years later.

Why I don't buy new one? First, because it is cheaper. New boots is very expensive, maybe one hundred and sixty pounds. And second, because these boots know my feet already. New boots always make problem in the beginning. Also I don't like to throw away things which are still good. So this is why I repaired my boots.

what_caps_it.point: Duration, subject–verb agreement and the past tense all break in the same three sentences.
'Very good', 'very expensive', 'make problem' — the description never leaves school vocabulary.
Reasons arrive as a numbered list, and every other sentence starts with 'and' or 'so'.

annotations.span: these boots know my feet already
annotations.label: One genuinely vivid image
annotations.why: Keep this exactly as it is — it is the most memorable line in the answer.

annotations.span: I have them since that time
annotations.label: Present perfect duration missing
annotations.why: Say 'I've had them for about nine years' and the whole opening steadies.

annotations.span: my foot is wet every time I go outside
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past account
annotations.why: It should be 'my foot was getting wet every time I went out'.

annotations.span: New boots is very expensive
annotations.label: Plural subject with a singular verb
annotations.why: 'Boots are'. Check the noun the verb belongs to before you speak.

annotations.span: They are very good boots.
annotations.label: Flat adjective doing important work
annotations.why: Try 'they're heavier than anything sold now' — describe instead of rating.

annotations.span: So this is why I repaired my boots.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: End on what the choice tells you, not on the words of the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same object, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd like to talk about is a pair of walking boots — dark brown leather, quite heavy, the sort that take a fortnight to break in.

I've had them for about nine years now. I bought them for a walking trip I'd signed up to, and honestly I expected to wear them twice, but they've ended up being what I put on for most of the winter. There's a scar across the left toe from a loose stone, which I quite like, oddly enough.

What went wrong was the sole. It started letting water in about four years ago — nothing dramatic, just a damp sock at the end of a long day — and when I turned them over there was a split running the whole length of the seam. There's a cobbler in a railway arch near the station who resoled them for forty pounds, and he's done it once more since.

As for why I keep mending them rather than buying a new pair, part of it is the money, since a decent pair costs somewhere near a hundred and sixty. But the honest reason is that these ones fit. A new pair means a fortnight of blisters, whereas these already know exactly what my feet are like. And there's a third thing, which is that throwing out something that still works feels wrong to me, even when it turns out to be the cheaper option.

So that's the case for repair in a nutshell — it isn't really about money at all.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect holds the duration, and 'whereas' joins two clauses where band 6 used 'and'.
'Break in', 'letting water in', 'in a nutshell' — chunks the band 6 had no access to.
Three signposts and one concession make the reasoning audible instead of listed.

annotations.label: A relative clause carrying real content
annotations.why: Describe an object by what it does to you, not by an adjective.

annotations.span: I've had them for about nine years now.
annotations.label: Present perfect with a duration
annotations.why: Any possession card wants this in the first fifteen seconds.

annotations.span: dark brown leather, quite heavy
annotations.label: Two descriptors as one breath group
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across both, then pause before the next idea.

annotations.span: What went wrong was the sole.
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Five words tell the listener a new section has started.

annotations.span: It started letting water in about four years ago
annotations.label: The verb a native speaker would use
annotations.why: 'Let water in' beats 'was broken' on any container or piece of clothing.

annotations.span: As for why I keep mending them rather than buying a new pair
annotations.label: Announces the fourth bullet out loud
annotations.why: Naming the move is what stops you forgetting the 'explain' bullet.

annotations.span: whereas these already know exactly what my feet are like
annotations.label: 'Whereas' linking two full clauses
annotations.why: Reach for 'whereas' the second time you would have said 'but'.

annotations.span: And there's a third thing, which is that
annotations.label: Counts the reasons as they arrive
annotations.why: Numbering out loud buys thinking time and sounds organised, not listed.

annotations.span: So that's the case for repair in a nutshell
annotations.label: An idiom that closes the turn
annotations.why: One idiom at the end lands better than four scattered through.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'll take a pair of walking boots — dark brown leather, heavier than anything anyone sells now, and on their third sole.

They came into my life about nine years ago, for a trip I'd been talked into, and I assumed they'd go straight to the back of a cupboard afterwards. Instead they've become the thing I reach for from October onwards. There's a gouge across the left toe from a loose stone, which I've never had the slightest wish to hide.

The sole was the first thing to go. It began quietly — a damp sock, nothing you'd call a leak — and by the time I turned them over there was a split running the length of the seam. A cobbler works out of a railway arch near the station, and he resoled them for forty pounds without once suggesting I buy something else. He has done it again since.

Now, why not simply replace them? Money comes into it, of course; a comparable pair runs to something like a hundred and sixty. But that isn't what decides it. What decides it is that these have already made every adjustment a boot can make to one particular pair of feet, and no new pair arrives pre-worn.

If I'm honest there's a stubbornness in it too. Nothing about them has stopped working, and I have never been able to see the argument for replacing something on the grounds that it has merely got older.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft sentence carries the main reason, and a passive quietly removes the persuader.
'On their third sole', 'talked into', 'runs to' — compression, not extra words.
The close states a principle that the boots only happen to illustrate.

annotations.span: What decides it is that these have already made every adjustment
annotations.label: Cleft sentence fronting the real reason
annotations.why: 'What decides it is…' puts your best point in the strongest position.

annotations.span: for a trip I'd been talked into
annotations.label: Passive idiom in five words
annotations.why: It tells us somebody persuaded him without naming or explaining them.

annotations.span: on their third sole
annotations.label: Four words instead of a sentence
annotations.why: Compression like this is what band 8 sounds like, not rare words.

annotations.span: It began quietly — a damp sock, nothing you'd call a leak —
annotations.label: Parenthesis delivered at lower pitch
annotations.why: Drop the pitch inside the dashes, then come back up. It sounds unrehearsed.

annotations.span: I have never been able to see the argument for replacing something on the grounds that it has merely got older
annotations.label: Ends on a principle, not a summary
annotations.why: State the rule your story is an example of, then stop talking.

model_answers.transcript:
The problem I'd choose is the junction at the end of my road, right outside a primary school, where there's no proper crossing at all.

It's a fairly narrow road with cars parked hard against the kerb on both sides, and drivers come round the bend faster than they should, because there's nothing there to slow them down. If you're standing at the kerb with a child, you can't actually see what's coming until you're already halfway out. There are white lines painted on the tarmac and one sign, and that is the extent of it.

The people it hits hardest are the ones with the least room for error — small children walking in on their own from about the age of seven, parents pushing prams, and a few older neighbours. One of them, who's in her eighties, told me she'd started going the long way round rather than risk it, which is a fifteen-minute detour on a road she has lived on all her life.

Something was attempted, to be fair. A group of parents got a petition together a couple of years ago, and the response was the paint and the sign — a stopgap, essentially, and nothing that changes what a driver can see.

As for why it should be a priority, the fix is cheap, it's a set of lights, and everybody involved already knows that. What worries me is that these things tend to get done after somebody is hurt rather than before, and there's no good reason for that to be how it works.

model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd pick is the junction at the end of my road, immediately outside a primary school, which has never had a crossing on it.

It's a narrow street with cars wedged against the kerb on both sides, and since there's nothing to slow anybody down, drivers take the bend at a speed the road was never built for. Stand at that kerb holding a child's hand and you are effectively blind until you have already committed. What exists by way of protection is some paint and a sign.

The people carrying the risk are the ones least able to absorb it — seven-year-olds walking in alone, parents with prams, and a handful of neighbours in their eighties. One of them told me she now walks the long way round, a quarter of an hour's detour on a street she has lived on since she was married.

In fairness, something was tried. Parents put a petition in a couple of years back, and the paint and the sign were what came of it. Nobody involved would call that a solution; it is what gets done when a solution has been deferred.

What makes it worth pushing is that none of it is difficult. It needs a set of lights, and everybody knows as much. Had that junction sat outside a hospital or a courthouse, it would have been dealt with years ago. The problem isn't cost or complexity — it's that the people it endangers are the ones least able to make a fuss.

model_answers.label: The target — same square, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd pick is the old market square, right at the top of the high street, about two minutes from the bus station.

It's a wide open space paved in cobbles, with a stone fountain in the middle that hasn't run for years, and a set of broad steps that people treat as seating. On one side there's the market hall, which is basically a roof on pillars, so there's somewhere dry to stand when it rains — and that matters more than it sounds, given the weather we get.

Who you find there depends entirely on the hour. First thing, it's older men playing chess on the two stone tables under the hall roof, and they're out there almost regardless of the temperature. From about four it belongs to teenagers, who sit along the steps in a row and are audible from the far end of the street on a quiet afternoon. Sundays it fills up with families, mostly because the fountain is the one thing small children can be trusted around.

As for why people choose it over anywhere else, the honest answer is that it costs nothing and nobody moves you on. In the shopping centre you're expected to be buying something, whereas nobody in the square has ever asked me what I'm doing there. And it's on the way to everything, so meeting there isn't a detour for anybody.

I think that's what a public space actually is — somewhere you can turn up without a reason.

I'll take the old market square, at the top of the high street and a couple of minutes' walk from the bus station.

It's a wide cobbled space with a stone fountain at its centre, dry for as long as I can remember, and a run of shallow steps that everybody uses as seating without anyone ever having decided they should. Along one edge stands the market hall — a roof held up on pillars, essentially — which gives you somewhere to stand out of the rain, and in a town with our weather that is not a small thing.

I'll talk about the time I needed to see a doctor, which was in February, a few weeks after I'd moved cities for work.

I'd had earache for about three days and it had got to the point where I couldn't sleep on that side. The trouble was that I hadn't registered with a surgery yet, so there was no appointment for me to book in the first place. A colleague mentioned a walk-in centre next to the leisure centre, and that looked like the only option left.

I got there just before eight and there was already a queue down the side of the building. I waited about two hours, and then the woman on the desk announced that they'd reached capacity for the day. Which, honestly, was the point at which I nearly gave up and went home.

What she did instead was pick up the phone. She rang round three or four surgeries in the area, explained the situation each time, and found one that would take me at four that afternoon. It took her about fifteen minutes, and none of it was her job.

As for how I felt about it — grateful to her personally, and fairly cross with everything around her. That's what I took away from it, really. The service was clearly stretched to breaking point, whereas the person inside it went out of her way for somebody she'd never met. Those two facts sat side by side all morning, and I don't think one cancels out the other.

model_answers.transcript:
This is about needing a doctor in February, a few weeks into a move I'd made for work.

I'd been carrying an earache around for three days by then, and it had reached the stage where lying on that side was out of the question. Having only just arrived, I wasn't registered anywhere, which meant there was no appointment for me to book at all. A colleague pointed me towards a walk-in centre beside the leisure centre, and I went on the basis that it was that or nothing.

I was there shortly before eight, behind a queue that already ran the length of the building. Two hours later the woman on the desk announced that they had hit capacity for the day, which is roughly when I decided to write the morning off.

Rather than leave it there, she picked up the phone. She worked through three or four surgeries, explaining the whole thing again each time, and found one prepared to see me at four. Fifteen minutes of her day, and not a second of it was anything she was obliged to do.

What stays with me is how easily those two things sat together. The service itself was visibly running on empty; the person staffing it went well past anything anyone could have asked for. It would be neat to conclude that the second redeems the first, and I have never quite managed to believe that it does.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a rule in the trains in my country. In every long train there is one carriage which is called the quiet carriage. In this carriage you cannot make phone call and you cannot listen music loud.

The rule is only in this one carriage, not in the whole train. There is a sign in the window and also a small sign inside, near the door. I think it is always the first or the last one.

About how people follow it, I would say quite good. Sometimes somebody forget and takes a call, but then all the people look at him and he goes outside to the corridor. The staff never say nothing about it, it is the passengers who do it.

I think this rule is good because it is not expensive for the company. They only put a sign. And for the passengers it is very relaxing, you can sleep or read. 'Good', 'not expensive', 'very relaxing' — the defence rests on three plain adjectives.
The objection appears in one sentence at the end and is dropped without an answer.

annotations.why: Keep this — 'it is X who…' is exactly the structure the argument needed.

annotations.span: you cannot listen music loud

annotations.span: Sometimes somebody forget and takes a call
annotations.label: Third-person -s on one verb only
annotations.why: 'Somebody forgets and takes a call.' Both verbs share the subject.

annotations.why: 'The staff never say anything.' English allows one negative per clause.

model_answers.label: The target — same rule, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The rule I'd like to talk about is the quiet carriage on the trains here — no phone calls, no music out loud, and conversation kept fairly low.

It only applies to one carriage on each of the longer trains, usually the one at the very front or the very back. There's a sticker on the outside of the window and another one by the door, so you can't board it by accident and claim you didn't know. Everywhere else on the train you can do more or less as you please.

How strictly it's followed is the interesting part, because it's almost entirely self-policing. The staff don't enforce it at all — I've never once seen a guard say a word. What happens instead is that somebody takes a call, and within about ten seconds half the carriage has looked up, and the person concerned is on their feet and heading for the door, still talking. Nobody has to say anything. It works far better than a fine would.

As for why it does more good than harm, I'd accept straight away that it's an inconvenience if you genuinely need to be reachable — but nothing forces you to sit there. That's the whole point of it: it's a choice rather than a ban. It costs the operator nothing beyond two stickers, and it gives you an hour when nobody can get hold of you, which is harder to come by than it used to be.

The best rules seem to be the ones nobody has to enforce.

'Self-policing', 'come by', 'get hold of you' — chunks doing what adjectives did before.
The objection is raised and answered inside the turn instead of left hanging.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The rule I'd choose is the quiet carriage on our intercity trains — no calls, no music aloud, conversation at a murmur.

It covers exactly one carriage per train, generally the one at either end, and it's announced by a sticker on the window and a second one inside the door. Nobody ends up in there by mistake; if they do, they have walked past two warnings to manage it. The rest of the train is left entirely alone, and always has been.

What interests me is that nothing enforces it. In all the years I've been using those trains I have never seen a guard intervene. Somebody's phone goes, they answer it, and inside ten seconds a carriage of strangers has looked up in unison — at which point the offender is on their feet and heading for the door, still talking. Not a word is exchanged. No penalty ever devised would work that fast.

Does it cost anybody anything? Certainly, if you need to be reachable — though nothing compels you to sit there, and that is precisely what makes it defensible. It is opt-in. Against that, it costs the operator two stickers and hands passengers an hour in which they cannot be found, which is a scarcer commodity every year.

I've come to think that's the mark of a rule worth having: it survives on the strength of what everybody already believes, and the enforcement is only ever a formality.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about the time when I helped in a running event in my village. It is every year in May, and many people from other places come also.

I helped because my neighbour asked me. Two days before, she called me and she said one person cannot come, so they need somebody. I said okay because I have nothing special to do that day.

My job was the water. I was in the table at four kilometres. Before the start I filled the cups with water, maybe four hundred cups, it took long time. And then when the runners come, I give them the cup. It was very busy for one hour. Some people take the cup and throw it on the ground, and after we must pick up everything.

What I got from this? I think two things. First, now I know many people in my village. Before I only know my neighbours. And second, I understand that somebody must do the boring job. It is not interesting but without this the event cannot happen. So I was happy to help.

what_caps_it.point: Four verbs slip into the present tense, and two nouns lose their article.
'Very busy', 'boring', 'happy' — two hours of work described in three words.
'First' and 'second' are the only cohesion; nothing else links one sentence to the next.

annotations.span: somebody must do the boring job
annotations.label: A real conclusion, not a summary
annotations.why: Keep the idea and give it better words — this is what the bullet was asking for.

annotations.span: I want to tell about the time
annotations.label: Wrong verb for the opening
annotations.why: 'Tell' needs a person: 'I'll tell you about…' or simply 'I'd like to talk about…'.

annotations.span: I was in the table at four kilometres
annotations.label: Wrong preposition for a position
annotations.why: 'On the table' if it's an object, 'at the table' if it's your post.

annotations.span: it took long time
annotations.label: Article missing before a time phrase
annotations.why: 'It took a long time.' The article is not optional here.

annotations.span: when the runners come, I give them the cup
annotations.label: Past story told in the present
annotations.why: 'When the runners came, I handed them a cup.' Fix the tense once, early.

annotations.span: So I was happy to help.
annotations.label: A flat verdict closing the turn
annotations.why: You had a better ending two sentences earlier. Move it to the end.

model_answers.label: The target — same morning, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll tell you about the village fun run, which happens on the first Saturday in May and pulls in a few hundred people from the surrounding area.

I ended up involved almost by accident. My neighbour rang me on the Thursday evening to say that somebody had pulled out, and would I mind covering a water station. I'd never done anything like it before, but it was two hours on a Saturday morning, so it was quite hard to think of a reason not to.

What I actually did was less glamorous than it sounds. I was on the table at the four-mile mark, and the first job was filling cups — about four hundred of them, poured out in advance and lined up in rows, which took the best part of an hour before anybody had even set off. Then the runners came through in waves for about seventy minutes, and after that we spent half an hour picking cups out of the hedge.

What I got out of it wasn't what I expected. I'd assumed it would be a pleasant enough morning and nothing more. In fact the useful part is that I now recognise about forty people in the village that I'd only have nodded at before, which changes what walking to the shop feels like. The other thing, slightly less comfortably, is that I'd never once thought about who does the dull jobs at events I've enjoyed for years.

Somebody had always been filling those cups.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a reported question replace band 6's flat run of past simples.
'Pulls in', 'the best part of an hour', 'less glamorous than it sounds' — chunks, not adjectives.
Every paragraph names the bullet it is answering, and the last line carries the point.

annotations.span: I ended up involved almost by accident.
annotations.label: Answers the second bullet in six words
annotations.why: Say how you got involved before you say what you did; it explains the whole story.

annotations.span: somebody had pulled out, and would I mind covering a water station
annotations.label: Past perfect plus a reported question
annotations.why: Dropping the reporting verb — 'and would I mind' — is very natural spoken English.

annotations.span: pulls in a few hundred people
annotations.label: A verb that measures an event
annotations.why: 'Pull in' is what events do to crowds; reuse it for a festival or a match.

annotations.span: What I actually did was less glamorous than it sounds.
annotations.label: Signposts the third bullet
annotations.why: Announcing the bullet buys a second and stops you drifting off it.

annotations.span: which took the best part of an hour before anybody had even set off
annotations.label: Relative clause with a past perfect inside
annotations.why: Two time layers in one clause is exactly the range examiners are listening for.

annotations.span: picking cups out of the hedge
annotations.label: The detail that proves you were there
annotations.why: One unglamorous specific does more than any adjective for credibility.

annotations.span: What I got out of it wasn't what I expected.
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluative bullet
annotations.why: This is the bullet that carries the band. Never let it arrive unannounced.

annotations.span: I'd assumed it would be a pleasant enough morning
annotations.label: Past perfect for a mistaken expectation
annotations.why: 'I'd assumed…' sets up a contrast the listener is now waiting for.

annotations.span: Somebody had always been filling those cups.
annotations.label: One short sentence as the ending
annotations.why: End short. A six-word close after a long paragraph lands hard.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is the village fun run — first Saturday in May, a few hundred entrants, and rather more spectators than the village strictly has residents.

I was drafted in rather than volunteering, if I'm honest about it. My neighbour phoned on the Thursday to say somebody had dropped out and to ask whether I'd take a water station, and two hours of a Saturday is not something you can refuse without sounding as though you have better things to do.

The work itself was as unglamorous as it gets. I had the table at four miles, and the first hour went entirely on filling cups — four hundred of them, poured and lined up before a single runner had left the start. Then seventy minutes of holding one out and having it taken, over and over, while people I had never met said thank you without breaking stride. Afterwards, half an hour retrieving cups from a hedge.

What I took from it was not the warm feeling I had been expecting. It was, first, that I now recognise perhaps forty faces I would previously have walked straight past, which quietly alters the business of going out for bread. And second, less comfortably, that I had spent years enjoying events of that kind without once wondering who filled the cups. Somebody always had.

I've done it every May since. Not out of virtue, particularly — more because, having once seen the machinery, it is quite difficult to unsee it.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause and the elliptical 'Somebody always had' do work band 7 spelled out.
'Drafted in', 'without breaking stride', 'the machinery' — one image, chosen rather than decorative.
The reason for going back is given last and undercuts itself, which sounds unrehearsed.

annotations.span: having once seen the machinery, it is quite difficult to unsee it
annotations.label: Participle clause carrying the reason
annotations.why: Front the cause as an -ing clause and the sentence stops sounding like a list.

annotations.span: I was drafted in rather than volunteering
annotations.label: One passive verb, whole situation
annotations.why: 'Drafted in' says asked, needed and not entirely willing, in two words.

annotations.span: as unglamorous as it gets
annotations.label: A superlative built from an idiom
annotations.why: 'As … as it gets' is the natural spoken superlative; use it once per turn.

annotations.span: holding one out and having it taken, over and over
annotations.label: Repetition delivered as one flat run
annotations.why: Keep the pitch level across the repeat; the monotony is the meaning.

annotations.span: Somebody always had.
annotations.label: Three words, whole point
annotations.why: Ellipsis at the end of a paragraph is the most controlled ending available.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I want to talk about is the weddings. In my country a wedding is very very expensive, more than people can pay I think.

Who spends the most? Normally the family of the bride pays for the biggest part, but now also the couple pay themselves, especially if they are older, maybe thirty or thirty-five.

Why it is so expensive? First because everybody invites so many guest. Two hundred, three hundred people is normal. And the food for this is a lot of money. Also the place, the hotel, they know the date is fixed, so they don't reduce the price. My cousin married last year and it cost more than fifteen thousand, only for one day.

Is it money well spent? For me, no. Because after one day it is finished, but the loan is not finished. They pay for three years. Of course the family is happy and the photos are nice. But I think it is too much. So this is something people spend a lot of money on in my country.

what_caps_it.point: A plural is dropped, a plural subject takes a singular verb, and 'the' opens a generalisation.
'Very very expensive', 'a lot of money', 'too much' — one idea wearing three costumes.
Each bullet is read out as a question and answered separately; the answers never join up.

annotations.span: The thing I want to talk about is the weddings.

annotations.why: Repeating 'very' adds nothing. 'Eye-watering' or a number adds a lot.

annotations.label: Plural -s missing after a quantifier
annotations.why: 'So many guests'. 'Many' guarantees the noun is plural.

model_answers.label: The target — same subject, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd pick is weddings, which have got extraordinarily expensive here over the last twenty years or so.

Traditionally it was the bride's family who paid for most of it, and to a large extent that's still the case, though couples now tend to be older — often well into their thirties — and end up funding a fair chunk of it themselves. So it's usually two households and one couple all contributing, which is part of why nobody ever quite adds up the total.

As for why it costs what it does, I'd say there are two reasons. The obvious one is the guest list: two or three hundred people is normal, and once you're feeding that many, everything else scales with it. The less obvious one is that the date gets fixed months in advance, so the venue and the caterer know perfectly well you can't walk away. Nobody haggles over a wedding. A cousin of mine got married last spring and the whole thing came to somewhere over fifteen thousand, for a single day.

Is it money well spent? Honestly, I don't think it is — although I'd want to be careful here, because it clearly matters enormously to the people doing it. My objection is narrower than that. The day lasts twelve hours and the borrowing lasts three years, and I've watched more than one couple start married life in debt to impress relatives they see twice a decade.

If it were really about the marriage, nobody would need the flowers.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect for the change and a second conditional for the close, where band 6 had neither.
'A fair chunk', 'scales with it', 'haggles' — precision instead of three kinds of 'expensive'.
The two reasons are ranked out loud, and the judgement is hedged before it is delivered.

annotations.span: which have got extraordinarily expensive here over the last twenty years
annotations.label: Present perfect for a change
annotations.why: Any 'how things are now' card wants one present perfect in its first sentence.

annotations.span: end up funding a fair chunk of it themselves
annotations.label: Two chunks in one clause
annotations.why: 'End up -ing' and 'a fair chunk' are both reusable anywhere money is discussed.

annotations.span: As for why it costs what it does, I'd say there are two reasons.
annotations.label: Signposts and counts at once
annotations.why: Promising two reasons obliges you to give two, which stops you drifting.

annotations.span: everything else scales with it
annotations.label: One verb explains the arithmetic
annotations.why: 'Scales with' says 'goes up in proportion' in three words.

annotations.span: The less obvious one is that
annotations.label: Ranks the second reason above the first
annotations.why: Saying which reason is better is analysis; listing two is not.

annotations.span: Nobody haggles over a wedding.
annotations.label: Five words, delivered as a full stop
annotations.why: A short sentence after a long one resets the listener's attention.

annotations.span: although I'd want to be careful here
annotations.label: Hedges before criticising
annotations.why: It signals you know real people are involved, and it costs you nothing.

annotations.span: My objection is narrower than that.
annotations.label: Narrows the claim on purpose
annotations.why: A precise small objection is far harder to argue with than a sweeping one.

annotations.span: If it were really about the marriage, nobody would need the flowers.
annotations.label: Second conditional closing the turn
annotations.why: End on a conditional and the examiner hears grammar and judgement together.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
I'd choose weddings, which within my lifetime have gone from expensive to something close to absurd.

The money still comes largely from the bride's family, by custom, but the picture has blurred. People marry later now, often well into their thirties, and a couple who have both been earning for a decade end up carrying a good deal of it themselves. Three sets of pockets, one bill, and nobody with a complete view of the total.

Why so much? Partly arithmetic. Invite three hundred people and every other decision is multiplied by three hundred before you have even made it. But the sharper reason is that the date is set long before the money is spent, and everybody selling into that day knows it. There is no walking away from a booked venue six weeks out, and the prices reflect precisely that, as everyone in the trade understands. A cousin married last spring for something north of fifteen thousand, which bought one afternoon.

Well spent? I'd say not, though I want to be careful, because for the people involved it plainly is. What I object to is narrower: the celebration lasts an afternoon and the repayments last three years, and I have watched couples begin a marriage in debt in order to impress relatives they will next see at a funeral.

Strip out everything nobody would notice was missing, and what you'd have left is the part that was actually the wedding.

what_lifts_it.point: An imperative used as a conditional, and a verbless sentence carrying a paragraph's whole point.
'North of', 'three sets of pockets', 'arithmetic' — compression rather than extra vocabulary.
The close proposes a test instead of a verdict, and lets the listener finish it.

annotations.span: Invite three hundred people and every other decision is multiplied by three hundred
annotations.label: Imperative doing a conditional's job
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is a conditional without the 'if'. Very natural, very spoken.

annotations.span: something north of fifteen thousand
annotations.label: An approximator that sounds native
annotations.why: 'North of' means 'more than' and signals you're estimating, not quoting.

annotations.span: Three sets of pockets, one bill
annotations.label: A verbless sentence doing real work
annotations.why: Cut the verb when the nouns alone carry the idea. It sounds thought, not read.

annotations.span: Why so much? Partly arithmetic.
annotations.label: Question and fragment, tight rhythm
annotations.why: Ask your own question, answer it in two words, then expand. It resets the pace.

annotations.span: Strip out everything nobody would notice was missing
annotations.label: Ends by proposing a test
annotations.why: Give the listener a way to check your claim and the claim sounds earned.
